title: Who Is the Second Cup For?
brief: The new drink goes on sale at 8 tomorrow morning. Kai brings you an AI interview summary and asks what No-Overtime Milk Tea should lead with.

lines.text: The AI put “worried it’ll be too sweet” at the top of its summary of the walk-up interviews at Lanshan Plaza. You’re the planner. Would you lead with that?
The client’s already stuck “Less Sugar” on the menu board. He wants an answer by five.
I spent half an hour at the Songgao Road shop. This woman ordered half sugar, so why did she add another cup just before paying?
Hang on, I’ll pull up the transcript. She said, “I was worried my coworker would find it too sweet.” Yep, two different sugar levels.
I asked her about it. Her coworker was still wrapping up a project, so she was taking a cup back to give them a break.
Okay, I’ll get them to hold the menu board. We owe the client a line he can put on it by five.

steps.prompt: The client needs the wording locked by five. What do you do with the receipt and interview?

options.text: Lead with “Bring a cup to someone still working.” Interview the evening crowd, then give that line the space reserved for the discount.
options.feedback: You finish typing up the extra interviews after closing, and Wei stays with you until almost dawn to get the wording right. The next day, someone snaps a photo of the line and sends it to a coworker, but you lose the orders a launch discount would have brought in.
options.insight: The yearbook warns that when everyone uses the same AI, the work tends toward the average. A team with varied talent is what gives a business a lasting edge.

options.text: Play the recording for the client and compare the two sugar levels. Test “Choose the sweetness for each cup” at one shop first.
options.feedback: You and Kai cross-check receipts half the evening, and the client crosses out “Less Sugar” himself after hearing the recording. The test shop gets a few extra two-cup orders, and the client asks you to run the next round of interviews.
options.insight: The yearbook calls first-party data the foundation for making money with AI. Poor-quality input leads to poor-quality output.

options.text: Launch tomorrow morning with NT$10 off the second cup. Save the coworker message for the next campaign.
options.feedback: Two-cup orders take off in the morning, but by lunch all anyone is sharing in group chats is a screenshot of the discount. The client asks what you’ll say next time without a deal, and you’re still sorting through comments after closing.
options.insight: The yearbook identifies four kinds of friction for shoppers: money, time, physical effort, and mental effort. Generative AI is especially good at saving mental effort.
